title: Is the Letter Really Dead?
blurb: Talk about written communication, past and present

steps.html:
Nobody writes letters any more — except that stationery shops are having their best years in decades. Two short texts, and the tense that holds the past and the present together.

  • Read two texts for main idea, detail and inference
  • Use the present perfect simple and continuous accurately
  • Write about your own history with letters and messages

steps.title: The box in the hallway
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 142 words

My grandmother has kept every letter she has ever received. They sit in a wooden box in her hallway, tied with string. I have been going through them since March, and I have found things no inbox could ever hold: a shopping list, an apology, a line of poetry copied out in careful handwriting.

Digital media has changed correspondence completely. I have been writing to my closest friends for fifteen years, but almost all of it has been instant — a message sent, read and deleted inside the same minute. Nothing survives. My grandmother's letters have been sitting in that box since 1961 and they have not lost a single word.

I have not written a handwritten letter since school. This week I have been trying to change that, and I have already discovered how slow my own hand has become.

steps.title: What is the writer's main point?
options: Digital messages are harder to write than letters.
Digital messages disappear, while letters survive.
Her grandmother wrote better letters than anyone else.
steps.answer: Digital messages disappear, while letters survive.
steps.why: The contrast runs through the text: a message is 'sent, read and deleted inside the same minute', while the letters 'have not lost a single word'.

steps.title: Why the pen is selling again
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 147 words

Stationery sales have been rising for three years, and nobody in the industry has been expecting it. Shops that have sold pens and paper since the 1950s have suddenly become fashionable again.

Rachel Innes, who has run a stationery shop in York since 2004, thinks she knows why. 'People have been staring at screens all day. A postage stamp, good paper, real punctuation — it slows you down. You cannot cross out a word without leaving a mark, so you think before you write.'

She has noticed something else. 'Nobody has ever put an emoticon in a letter. You haven't got one, so you have to say what you mean.' Her customers have been buying more confidential, personal paper this year than at any time she can remember. Her own in tray, she admits, has been overflowing since November.

steps.title: Answer the questions.
steps.prompt: Why does Rachel Innes think people are buying paper again?
options: Because paper has become cheaper than screens.
Because writing by hand is slower and makes you think first.
Because employers now require handwritten letters.
steps.answer: Because writing by hand is slower and makes you think first.
steps.why: 'It slows you down… so you think before you write.'

steps.title: What each form is for
steps.html:
The full rule first, then a large example bank, then practice.

Both forms connect the past to now. The difference is what you are pointing at.

Present perfect simple (have / has + past participle) points at a completed action, a result, or a quantity: I have found three letters. The letters are found; you can count them.

Present perfect continuous (have / has been + -ing) points at the activity itself and how long it has gone on, whether or not it is finished: I have been going through the box since March. You are still going through it.

Ask yourself: am I saying how many (simple), or how long (continuous)?

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences, taken from or built on the two texts.

My grandmother has kept every letter she ever received.
Simple — a completed, permanent result.

I have been going through them since March.
Continuous — an activity still under way.

I have found a shopping list and an apology.
Simple — you can count what was found.

Digital media has changed correspondence completely.
Simple — one finished change with a present result.

I have been writing to my friends for fifteen years.
Continuous with for — duration.

The letters have been sitting in that box since 1961.
Continuous with since — a state stretched over time.

They have not lost a single word.
Simple — the negative of a result.

Stationery sales have been rising for three years.
Continuous — a trend, not a finished event.

Nobody in the industry has been expecting it.
Continuous — an ongoing state of mind over the period.

Rachel has run the shop since 2004.
Simple with a long time reference — normal with run, live, work, teach.

Nobody has ever put an emoticon in a letter.
Simple with ever — experience up to now.

Her customers have been buying more paper this year.
Continuous — repeated action across an unfinished period.

steps.title: State verbs, and for / since
steps.html:
State verbs — know, believe, own, mean, understand, seem, need, want — are not normally used in the continuous. Say I have known her for ten years, not I have been knowing her.

For is followed by a length of time: for three years, for twenty minutes, for ages. Since is followed by a point in time: since March, since 1961, since I left school.

A few verbs — live, work, study, teach, run — take either form with almost no change in meaning: She has worked / has been working here since 2004.

With always, never, ever, already, yet, just, use the simple: I have already discovered…, Nobody has ever put…

steps.title: Choosing between the two forms
steps.html:
1. The sentence: Sales ___ (rise) for three years.
  2. Ask how many or how long? The phrase for three years answers how long, so this points at duration.
  3. Duration and an unfinished trend mean the continuous: have been rising.
  4. Check the verb is not a state verb. Rise is an action, so the continuous is allowed: Sales have been rising for three years.
  5. Compare: Sales have risen by 12%. Here by 12% is a quantity, so the simple is right.

steps.title: You are going to write about your own written communication.
steps.sub: Which two will you build the piece around?

options.label: The last handwritten thing you kept
Something you have deleted and regretted
A person you have been writing to for years
Why you have stopped, or started, writing by hand

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 130–160 words. Use at least four words from this lesson, at least two present perfect simple forms and at least two continuous forms.
steps.html:
• Open with the situation now.
  • Second paragraph: what has been going on over a longer period.
  • Third paragraph: one thing you have or have not done, and why.
  • Use <i>since</i> and <i>for</i> at least once each.

Useful language

  • I have been … since / for …
  • I have never / already / just …
  • Nothing has changed as much as …
  • I have kept … , but I have deleted …
  • It has been … years since I last …
steps.modelHtml:
What I have kept

I have been using the same email address since 2009, and in that time my inbox has swallowed almost everything. I have deleted messages I would now pay to read. Nothing survives digital media unless you decide, on the day, that it should.

The one exception is a shoebox under my bed. My aunt has been writing to me since I moved abroad — one letter a month, always on the same blue stationery, always in handwriting I could recognise anywhere. I have kept every one of them. I have never once thought about throwing them away.

I have not answered the last three, which I am not proud of. This month I have been trying to catch up.
